correctness.rationale: Unit apex bonds can be gauged to 1, so H^2 applied to the apex has components (N,B1) and its squared norm is N^2+||B1||^2. The survival-probability t^4 coefficient is N^2/4+(N^2+||B1||^2)/12, since the first moment vanishes and the cubic term is imaginary. Thus matching cos^2 forces B1=0, and conversely this condition makes the apex and the normalized uniform base vector an invariant two-level system. Its population at t*=pi/(2 sqrt N) is uniform on the base, and Delta H=sqrt N at the apex establishes the speed-limit normalization. At a midpoint the two cubic-end phases are opposite; at each cubic vertex the three phases are a rotated cube-root triple. Their common cube therefore changes sign across each original edge, ruling out odd cycles. In a bipartite cubic graph Hall's theorem gives a perfect matching, and the remaining even cycles admit two alternating colors. These colors yield the phases and all row sums vanish. Connectedness propagates one triple to the whole first part and the negative triple to the second. Fixing one edge to have color 0 chooses exactly one representation of each phase assignment and exhibits the separate circles, indexed by labeled proper colorings modulo cyclic relabeling. In particular uniqueness is modulo the explicit cyclic identification, not uniqueness of unconstrained parameters. The frozen finite verification is corroboration, not a proof of nonexistence in infinitely many graphs; the reconstructed argument handles that obstruction. No extra gauge quotient or non-unit or weighted extension is asserted.

originality.rationale: There is verified equivalent coverage of the central theorem. After the prior apex-gauge row-sum characterization, the midpoint equations are exactly the identification of chiral phases with a unit complex Kirchhoff flow on the unsubdivided graph. Thomassen's 2014 Proposition 1 explicitly states that a cubic graph admits such a flow iff it is bipartite. Its proof already normalizes a nonzero flow on one edge to 1 and forces cube-root values and source/sink orientations. For fixed bipartition this is the labeled proper 3-edge-coloring normal form; putting the common rotation back and fixing an anchor-edge color gives the claimed circles directly. The transport profile and uniform departure are results of the prior two-dimensional cone reduction. The distinct same-day bicyclic record concerns genuinely different base graphs and is not the basis for this decision.
